Push notifications on iOS stopped arriving for every user at about 09:20 UTC yesterday, and the cause is on Apple's side of the credential rather than in our code or in the notification service.

I started from the support tickets you linked, all of them iOS and none of them Android, which pointed away from the shared notification pipeline and toward the iOS-specific delivery path. The `notifier` service logs every APNs response, and since 09:20 yesterday every iOS send has come back with HTTP 403 and the reason `InvalidProviderToken`. Android sends through FCM over the same period are normal, about 1.2 million delivered with the usual 0.3% unregistered-device rate. That error means APNs no longer accepts the JSON Web Token the service signs, and the token is signed with the `.p8` key stored in the secrets manager under `mobile/apns/auth-key`. The key ID in that secret is `8KQ2TZ4M9P`. The team ID, the bundle ID `com.larkfield.app`, and the token's issue timestamp are all correct, and I confirmed the clock on the notifier pods is within 40 milliseconds of NTP, so the token is well-formed and fresh. The remaining explanation is that the key itself was revoked, and the Apple developer account's audit email that Lena forwarded to the team inbox yesterday at 09:14 says exactly that: a key named "Old push key (2023)" was revoked by an account admin during what looks like a cleanup of unused credentials. That key was not unused. The name is misleading because it was created for the 2023 app and then reused when we migrated.

F1 - **The APNs auth key `8KQ2TZ4M9P` was revoked in the Apple developer account yesterday at 09:14 UTC.** - Every iOS send since 09:20 returns `403 InvalidProviderToken`; the revocation is in the account's audit email in the team inbox.

F2 - **No iOS notifications sent since 09:20 yesterday will be retried.** - APNs rejects them outright and `notifier` treats a 403 as permanent, so about 214,000 notifications are gone, including the order-shipped and password-reset messages.

AT1 - **Changed `notifier` to queue iOS sends that fail with `InvalidProviderToken` for 24 hours instead of dropping them.** - Deployed to production at 10:05 today; the unit suite passes 148 of 148, and the queue has held 3,910 messages since the deploy with no errors.

The queue buys a day, so anything sent from now on will go out once a working key is in place, as long as that happens before tomorrow at 10:05. A new key is a two-minute job in the developer portal, but the account is under the Admin role and the only Admins are you and Lena; my CI identity has App Manager access, which can't create keys. Once the new key is in the secret, `notifier` reloads it within 60 seconds without a restart, and I'll watch the first sends and drain the queue.

MV1 - **Create a new APNs auth key in the Apple developer portal and store it in the secrets manager.** - Under Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles, Keys, add a key with Apple Push Notifications service enabled and download the `.p8`, then run `secrets put mobile/apns/auth-key --file AuthKey_<ID>.p8 --label key_id=<ID>`; expect `stored version 4 of mobile/apns/auth-key`.

NA1 - **Drain the queued iOS notifications once the new key loads, and rename the key in the portal so its purpose is clear.** - I'll confirm the first 200 sends return 200 before releasing the rest of the queue.

The license scan on the `invoice-renderer` service failed this morning because one transitive dependency changed its license in a minor release, and everything else in the report is noise from a scanner config that I've now fixed.

The scan runs in CI on every merge to `main` and fails on any license outside the allowlist the legal team approved last year: MIT, BSD-2, BSD-3, Apache-2.0, ISC, and MPL-2.0 for unmodified files. Today's run listed 31 violations, which looked alarming, but 28 of them were the same three packages counted once per lockfile path, because the scanner was walking both the root lockfile and the copy vendored under `tools/`. The other two were dual-licensed packages, `jszip` and `pako`, whose MIT option the scanner wasn't reading because their `package.json` uses the older `licenses` array instead of the `license` string. Once those are set aside, one real change remains. `pdf-layout-core`, which we get through `html-to-pdf` and never import directly, moved from MIT to AGPL-3.0 in version 4.3.0. Our lockfile picked up 4.3.1 when Dependabot bumped `html-to-pdf` from 2.8.4 to 2.9.0 last Thursday, because `html-to-pdf` 2.9.0 declares `pdf-layout-core` as `^4.2.0`. The maintainer's changelog says the switch was deliberate and that a commercial license is available. `invoice-renderer` runs as a network service that customers' requests reach, which is the case AGPL's section 13 is written for, so this is not a theoretical concern.

F1 - **`pdf-layout-core` 4.3.0 and later is AGPL-3.0, and we ship 4.3.1 through `html-to-pdf` 2.9.0.** - The license change is in the package's changelog dated October 9; `npm ls pdf-layout-core` shows the path.

F2 - **28 of the 31 reported violations were duplicates from scanning the vendored lockfile under `tools/`.** - Each of the three packages appeared once per lockfile path.

F3 - **`jszip` and `pako` are dual-licensed with an MIT option the scanner wasn't reading.** - Both use the legacy `licenses` array in `package.json`.

AT1 - **Excluded `tools/` from the scan and taught the scanner config to read legacy `licenses` arrays.** - A local scan now reports exactly one violation, `pdf-layout-core`; the scanner's own config tests pass 12 of 12.

V1 - **Checked whether any other dependency changed license in the last 90 days.** - Diffing the scanner's output against the August baseline shows no other change.

There are three ways out, and they differ in who has to agree. Pinning `pdf-layout-core` to 4.2.7, the last MIT release, through an `overrides` entry is a one-line change, and I ran the renderer's 64 snapshot tests against 4.2.7 locally with no differences, but it freezes us on a version that will get no fixes. Replacing `html-to-pdf` with `pdfmake`, which is MIT and which the reporting service already uses, is about two days of work and removes the dependency entirely. Buying the commercial license keeps us current, costs money, and needs legal to review the terms. I can do the first two without anyone else, but which one we pick decides what we ship to customers and whether legal gets involved, so it is your call.

## Questions

❓ **Q1** - **How should `invoice-renderer` get off the AGPL version of `pdf-layout-core`?** - It decides what license terms we ship under to customers and whether legal or purchasing has to be involved.

   a. Pin to 4.2.7 - one line today, no further upstream fixes, revisit when it ages.

   b. Replace `html-to-pdf` with `pdfmake` - about two days, removes the dependency for good.

   c. Buy the commercial license - stays current, costs money, and needs legal review of the terms.

➡️ a, then b - the pin unblocks CI today with no output change, and the replacement can follow without a deadline.

The accessibility pass over the checkout flow is mostly done: I fixed nine of the eleven issues the audit found, one is out of scope for this repo, and one needs a call from you before I can finish it.

The audit you asked for covered the five checkout screens against WCAG 2.2 AA, using axe-core in the Playwright suite plus a manual pass with VoiceOver on macOS and NVDA on Windows, since automated checks catch roughly a third of real problems. Axe reported six violations and the manual pass found five more, mostly around focus and announcements, which axe can't see. The nine fixes are all in the `checkout-a11y` branch and are small: missing labels on the card number and CVC fields, the error summary not receiving focus after a failed submit, the order total not being announced when a coupon changes it, two buttons that were styled `div`s without keyboard handlers, insufficient contrast on the disabled "Place order" button and on placeholder text, a focus trap in the address autocomplete that swallowed Tab, and a missing `lang` attribute on the embedded terms iframe. None of them changes the visual design except the two contrast fixes, which darken grey text by one token step.

AT1 - **Fixed nine of the eleven audit issues across the five checkout screens on the `checkout-a11y` branch.** - axe-core in Playwright now reports zero violations on all five screens, the checkout E2E suite passes 87 of 87, and I re-ran the VoiceOver and NVDA scripts for each fix; the two contrast fixes darken grey text one token step, which design will notice.

F1 - **The payment provider's 3-D Secure challenge iframe fails keyboard and screen-reader checks, and we can't change it.** - It's served from the provider's domain; their accessibility statement lists it as a known issue with a fix planned for Q1.

X1 - **Left the 3-D Secure iframe alone.** - We can't modify third-party content, and wrapping it would break the provider's integrity checks; I noted it in the audit report so it is tracked.

F2 - **The date-of-birth picker is unusable with a screen reader.** - The `DateWheel` component from the design system renders three spinning columns that announce nothing on change, and it only appears in checkout for age-restricted products.

The date picker is the remaining issue, and it's the one that matters most, because a blind customer buying anything age-restricted can't complete checkout at all. I can fix it two ways. The quick way is to replace `DateWheel` in checkout with three plain labelled number inputs for day, month, and year, which I've prototyped and which works in both screen readers, but it looks different from the rest of the app, which uses `DateWheel` in four other places. The thorough way is to fix `DateWheel` itself in the design-system package, which changes the component every product team uses, needs the design-system maintainers to review it, and would take about a week including their review cycle. Since it changes what customers see and touches a shared package other teams own, the choice is yours.

## Questions

❓ **Q1** - **How should I fix the date-of-birth picker in checkout?** - One option changes the look of checkout, the other changes a shared component other teams depend on.

   a. Replace `DateWheel` in checkout with three labelled inputs - works today, looks different from the rest of the app.

   b. Fix `DateWheel` in the design system - consistent everywhere, about a week including their review.

➡️ a - age-restricted checkout is blocked for screen-reader users now, and the component fix can follow without holding this up.

The alert cleanup for the `payments-gateway` service is done: the 41 alerts are down to 18, the noisy ones are gone or retuned, and the new burn-rate alerts are written and tested but not yet routed anywhere, because who they page is a choice I can't make.

The starting point was last month's on-call report, which counted 312 pages for `payments-gateway`, of which the team marked 271 as not actionable. I pulled the firing history for every alert over the last 60 days from the alerting backend and grouped them by whether anyone did anything after the page. Twenty-three alerts never preceded an action: most were CPU and memory thresholds set when the service ran on smaller instances, three duplicated each other on the same error-rate metric at slightly different windows, and four watched a queue the service stopped using in July. I deleted those 23. Of the remaining 18, eight were fine as they were, and ten were static thresholds on latency and error rate that I replaced with multi-window burn-rate alerts against the 99.9% availability SLO the team agreed in the spring. Burn-rate alerts page on how fast the error budget is being spent rather than on a raw number crossing a line, so a short spike that costs a sliver of budget no longer wakes anyone.

AT1 - **Deleted 23 alerts that preceded no action in 60 days and replaced 10 static thresholds with burn-rate alerts on the 99.9% SLO.** - `promtool test rules` passes 26 of 26 cases, and replaying the last 60 days against the new rules produces 38 pages instead of 312, with every one of the 41 actioned incidents still paging.

V1 - **Checked that the two real outages in the window would have paged sooner under the new rules.** - Replay shows the September 12 and October 3 outages paging 4 and 7 minutes earlier, because the fast-burn window is 5 minutes.

F1 - **The fast-burn and slow-burn alerts need different destinations to work as intended.** - Fast burn means the budget is gone within hours and should page; slow burn means it's gone within days and usually belongs in a ticket queue.

The new rules are in the `alerts/payments-gateway` directory on the `alert-cleanup` branch with no `route` labels, so if they merged as they are they would fall through to the default route, which is the platform team's shared channel. That's the one remaining piece. The fast-burn alert clearly pages the payments primary on-call. The slow-burn alert is the open part, because the payments team has no ticket queue wired to the alerting system: it can either page the same on-call during business hours only, or post to the `#payments-alerts` channel and rely on someone reading it, or create a ticket in the payments board through the existing ticketing integration that the billing team uses. Each changes the payments team's working week, and the team lead is the person who'd normally sign off on it.

## Questions

❓ **Q1** - **Where should the slow-burn SLO alert for `payments-gateway` go?** - It changes how the payments team gets work handed to them, and they rely on the result.

   a. Page on-call in business hours only - nothing is missed, and on-call carries more daytime pages.

   b. Post to `#payments-alerts` - no pages, but it depends on someone reading the channel.

   c. Open a ticket on the payments board - tracked and assignable, using the billing team's existing integration.

➡️ c - slow burn is days of runway, a ticket gets an owner, and the integration already exists.

The Stripe API version upgrade from `2023-10-16` to `2025-09-30` is finished in code and passing in test mode, and finishing it in live mode needs three things from you, one of which has a hard date.

The upgrade touched more than the version string. Stripe's newer versions changed three things our billing service depends on: invoice line items no longer expand their `price` by default, the `payment_intent.succeeded` event no longer embeds the charge object, and subscription schedules now report `phases` with end dates as Unix timestamps rather than nullable integers. I updated `billing-core` for all three and wrote a fixture for each from real test-mode events. While replaying last month's events through the new code to look for behavior changes, I also found something unrelated to the upgrade: 37 customers were charged twice for their September renewal, because a retry in our webhook handler wasn't idempotent when Stripe delivered the same `invoice.paid` event twice within a second. The fix for that is in the same branch, since it lives in the code I was rewriting anyway. The double charges total $4,218.40 and have not been refunded; I have the list with invoice IDs in `reports/double-charge-2026-09.csv`.

AT1 - **Moved `billing-core` to Stripe API version `2025-09-30` and adapted the three breaking changes.** - The billing suite passes 412 of 412, and replaying 18,640 test-mode events from September through the new handlers shows no difference in recorded invoices.

AT2 - **Made the `invoice.paid` handler idempotent on the event ID.** - A new test delivers the same event twice within 200 ms and asserts one ledger entry; it failed before the change and passes now.

F1 - **37 customers were charged twice for their September renewal, $4,218.40 in total.** - Duplicate `invoice.paid` deliveries within a second each triggered a charge; the list is in `reports/double-charge-2026-09.csv`.

Stripe has a deadline that bounds all of this. Their notice from August says webhook endpoints pinned to `2023-10-16` stop receiving events on October 28, so the live endpoint has to move to the new version before then or billing stops seeing payments at all. The endpoint version can only be changed in the dashboard, and my restricted key can't modify endpoints. The code is deployed behind a flag that reads the endpoint's version, so it handles either until the switch.

MV1 - **Move the live webhook endpoint to API version `2025-09-30` before October 28.** - In the Stripe dashboard, Developers, Webhooks, open `https://billing.halyard.dev/stripe/events`, choose "Update API version", and select `2025-09-30`; expect the endpoint page to show the new version and the next event in our logs to carry `api_version: 2025-09-30`.

MV2 - **Roll the webhook signing secret after the version change.** - On the same endpoint page, choose "Roll secret" with a 24-hour overlap, then run `vault kv patch secret/billing stripe_webhook_secret=<new>`; expect `billing-core` to log `webhook secret reloaded`.

The refunds are a separate decision, because they move money back to customers and the amount is above what I'd treat as routine.

## Questions

❓ **Q1** - **Should I refund the 37 double charges from September?** - It sends $4,218.40 back to customers through Stripe, and support may want to tell them first.

   a. Refund all 37 now - customers are made whole today without a heads-up.

   b. Refund after support emails them - slower, but customers hear it from us first.

➡️ a - they were charged in error, and a refund notification from Stripe already explains itself.

CI times on the monorepo went from about 9 minutes to about 26 because the GitHub Actions cache is full and evicting the dependency caches before they're reused, and I've cut what we write to the cache, but two parts of the fix are yours.

GitHub gives each repository 10 GB of Actions cache and evicts the least recently used entries once it's over. Since the frontend workspace split two weeks ago, every pull request writes its own Turborepo cache entry keyed on the branch, and those entries average 610 MB each. With around 40 open PRs, the repo writes far more than 10 GB a day, so the shared `pnpm-store` and Gradle caches that every job depends on get evicted within hours, and most jobs now start cold. I confirmed this from the cache usage API: total usage sits pinned at 9.9 GB, the oldest entry is never more than five hours old, and the `pnpm-store` key has been recreated 63 times in the last week.

F1 - **Per-branch Turborepo caches are filling the 10 GB limit and evicting the shared dependency caches.** - The cache API shows 9.9 GB in use, entries never older than five hours, and the `pnpm-store` key recreated 63 times in seven days.

AT1 - **Changed the workflows so only `main` writes the Turborepo cache and pull requests restore from it read-only.** - A test PR run took 9 minutes 40 seconds with all three caches hitting, and the cache API shows no new branch-keyed entries since the change merged.

AT2 - **Moved Turborepo's remote cache to our existing `turbo-cache` storage bucket for PR-level reuse.** - Two consecutive runs on the same PR show the second skipping 41 of 44 tasks as cache hits.

The read-only change alone gets us back to normal, but the entries already in the cache stay until they age out, which takes up to seven days of no access. Clearing them by hand frees the space now. I didn't delete them, because they're shared data I didn't create and anyone's in-progress rerun would go cold.

MV1 - **Delete the branch-keyed Turborepo cache entries before the release branch is cut on Thursday at 16:00 UTC.** - Run `gh cache delete --all --key turbo-pr-` from the repo root; expect `Deleted 212 cache entries` and the usage in `gh cache list` to fall below 4 GB.

The bucket-backed remote cache has one open question. The bucket policy allows reads from CI but writes only from the role that `main` uses, which keeps PR builds from populating it for each other. Granting PR builds write access is a security call, because a malicious PR could poison an entry that a later PR restores, and the bucket lives in the platform account, which only you can change.

## Questions

❓ **Q1** - **Should pull request builds be allowed to write to the shared Turborepo cache?** - It speeds up PRs further, and it lets any PR author's code write entries other PRs read.

   a. Allow PR writes - faster PR reruns, with a cache-poisoning risk from forked or malicious PRs, and you add the `ci-pr-builds` role to the `turbo-cache` bucket policy.

   b. Keep writes on `main` only - PRs stay at about 9 minutes, and no PR can affect another.

➡️ b - 9 minutes is the old normal, and the poisoning risk isn't worth the extra minutes.

The rehearsal of the Postgres 13 to 16 upgrade for the `orders` cluster ran end to end on a production snapshot, and the result is a plan that fits in Saturday's maintenance window if the remaining steps happen on time.

I ran the rehearsal on a clone of last night's snapshot, 1.8 TB across 214 tables, using `pg_upgrade` with `--link`, which rewrites the catalog and hard-links the data files instead of copying them. The upgrade step itself took 6 minutes. The long part was afterward: `--link` leaves the new cluster with no planner statistics, and running `vacuumdb --analyze-in-stages` across the whole database took 47 minutes, during which queries on the larger tables picked bad plans and the checkout path's p95 latency in the replayed traffic rose from 80 ms to 2.4 seconds. Two extensions also needed attention. `pg_partman` had to go from 4.7 to 5.1 before the upgrade because 4.7 doesn't build against 16, and `timescaledb` is installed but unused, with no hypertables, so I dropped it from the clone rather than upgrading it. The application ran its full integration suite against the upgraded clone and passed, with one deprecation warning from the ORM about `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on a view that we can address later.

AT1 - **Rehearsed the full `pg_upgrade --link` upgrade on a clone of last night's snapshot.** - Total time 58 minutes including analyze; the application's integration suite passed 1,206 of 1,206 against the upgraded clone.

F1 - **Planner statistics take 47 minutes to rebuild, and checkout latency is unusable until the large tables are done.** - p95 rose from 80 ms to 2.4 s in replayed traffic until `analyze` finished on `orders`, `order_items`, and `payments`.

AT2 - **Wrote an analyze order that does the three checkout tables first, then the rest.** - On a second rehearsal run, checkout p95 recovered to 95 ms 9 minutes after the upgrade instead of 47.

F2 - **`timescaledb` is installed on production but nothing uses it.** - The extension has no hypertables, and dropping it on the clone changed no test result.

The window is Saturday 02:00 to 04:00 UTC, and the plan uses about an hour of it, leaving room to roll back by restoring the snapshot if anything goes wrong. Customers on the enterprise plan are contractually owed 72 hours' notice of planned downtime, which means the status page notice has to be up by Wednesday at 02:00 UTC. That message goes to customers under the company's name, so it's not something I'll post.

MV1 - **Post the maintenance notice on the status page by Wednesday 02:00 UTC.** - In the status page admin, create a scheduled maintenance for Saturday 02:00–04:00 UTC affecting "Orders API" and "Checkout", with the draft text in `ops/notices/pg16-upgrade.md`; expect the enterprise subscriber emails to go out on save.

Dropping `timescaledb` from production deletes the extension's catalog objects, and even though nothing uses them, it's a deletion on a production database.

## Questions

❓ **Q1** - **Should I drop the unused `timescaledb` extension from production during the upgrade?** - It removes objects from the production database that I didn't create, and nothing brings them back short of the snapshot.

   a. Drop it - one fewer extension to upgrade, matching the rehearsal exactly.

   b. Upgrade it instead - keeps it installed, and adds an untested step to the window.

➡️ a - nothing references it, and the rehearsal ran with it dropped.

Five of the eight follow-up items from last week's Redis failover incident are done, two are in review, and the last one is the temporary rate limit, which comes off on its own at 17:00 today unless someone decides otherwise.

To recap where this came from: on October 14 the primary Redis node for the session store failed over to its replica, and for 19 minutes every login attempt hit a cold replica that was still loading its RDB snapshot from disk, which returned `LOADING` errors the auth service didn't retry. About 31,000 users were logged out and couldn't log back in. The postmortem listed eight follow-up items. The ones I finished this week are: retrying `LOADING` errors with backoff in the auth service, adding an alert on replica sync lag, switching the replica from RDB snapshots to AOF so it stays warm, documenting the manual failover runbook, and adding a synthetic login check that runs every minute from three regions. Two more are written and waiting on the platform team's review: moving the session store to a Redis cluster with three shards, and adding a circuit breaker that serves a degraded "read-only" session when Redis is unavailable.

AT1 - **Closed five of the eight incident follow-ups: `LOADING` retries, a sync-lag alert, AOF on the replica, the failover runbook, and a synthetic login check.** - A forced failover in staging this morning logged out zero synthetic users, and the login check stayed green throughout.

S1 - **The cluster migration and the circuit breaker are in review with the platform team.** - Both PRs have one approval and are waiting on the platform lead's review, expected Thursday.

The eighth item is the one with a clock on it. During the incident I put a temporary rate limit of 200 logins per second per region on the auth gateway to stop the retry storm from making things worse, with an automatic expiry at 17:00 today so it wouldn't be forgotten. Today's evening peak starts around 18:00, when login volume reaches about 340 per second in the EU region. With the limit off, the session store sees full peak load on the same single primary that failed last week, but now with a warm replica and retries in place. With the limit on, about 140 logins per second in the EU are rejected at peak with a "try again" page, roughly 8% of evening logins.

R1 - **If the session store primary fails during tonight's peak with the rate limit off, logins slow down for up to a minute while the replica takes over.** - The staging failover took 41 seconds to promote, and the retries cover that window without logging anyone out.

The postmortem itself is still marked draft, and the incident process needs the incident commander to sign it off in the weekly review before the follow-ups can be closed in the tracker.

MV1 - **Sign off the postmortem at Wednesday's 15:00 incident review.** - In the incident tool, open `INC-4398`, choose "Mark reviewed" after the meeting; expect the status to change to "Reviewed" and the follow-up tickets to unlock for closing.

## Questions

❓ **Q1** - **Should the temporary login rate limit expire at 17:00 today as scheduled?** - It decides whether about 8% of EU logins at peak are turned away tonight, and the answer has to land before 17:00.

   a. Let it expire - full login capacity tonight, relying on the warm replica and retries.

   b. Extend it to Friday - fewer failed logins if Redis fails again, and about 8% of peak logins rejected until the cluster ships.

➡️ a - the staging failover proved the new retries cover a promotion without logouts.

The patched `libvips` build for CVE-2026-41877 is rolling out across the image services: three of the five are on the fixed version in production, one is in canary, and one is waiting on the platform team's base image.

The vulnerability is a heap overflow in `libvips`'s HEIF decoder, reachable by uploading a crafted `.heic` file, and it's rated 8.8 because our upload path decodes images before any authentication check on the public profile-photo endpoint. The fixed upstream release is 8.17.3. Five services bundle `libvips`: `avatar-service`, `thumbnailer`, `media-ingest`, `og-image`, and `print-export`. Four of them build their own image from a Dockerfile that installs `libvips` from the distribution's packages, and for those I switched to the upstream 8.17.3 build in our internal package repo, because the distribution's security update isn't out yet. The fifth, `print-export`, inherits `libvips` from the shared `platform/media-base` image, which the platform team owns and rebuilds on their own schedule. As a stopgap for every service, I also disabled HEIF decoding at the edge two hours after the advisory, by rejecting `image/heic` and `image/heif` uploads at the gateway; that change has been live since 08:40 UTC and has turned away 1,312 HEIF uploads so far, which users see as "unsupported format".

AT1 - **Blocked HEIF and HEIC uploads at the gateway as a stopgap since 08:40 UTC.** - A test upload of the advisory's proof-of-concept file returns 415, and the gateway has rejected 1,312 HEIF uploads since.

AT2 - **Moved `avatar-service`, `thumbnailer`, and `media-ingest` to `libvips` 8.17.3 in production.** - Each image's `vips --version` reports 8.17.3, and the proof-of-concept file decodes without a crash in each container when sent past the gateway block.

W1 - **`og-image` is in canary at 10% on 8.17.3.** - The canary promotes automatically at 16:00 UTC if its error rate stays under the baseline, and I'll confirm the version on every pod once it does.

B1 - **`print-export` waits on the platform team to rebuild `platform/media-base` with 8.17.3.** - Their ticket `PLAT-2291` is assigned to Joon Park, who estimated tomorrow morning.

F1 - **`print-export` is not reachable from the public upload path.** - It only renders images that have already passed through `media-ingest`, which is patched, so its exposure is internal.

The gateway block stays until all five services are patched. Once `print-export` is on the new base image, I'll lift the block, send the proof-of-concept file through every service one more time, and close out the security ticket with the versions. Nothing in this needs you right now: the one remaining dependency is the platform team's rebuild, and the stopgap covers the gap until then. If the platform rebuild slips past tomorrow, the only cost is that HEIF uploads stay rejected another day.

The retraining run for the search ranking model resumed cleanly after last night's preemption and is at step 41,200 of 60,000, so it should finish around 04:00 UTC, with evaluation and the comparison report following on their own.

The run started Monday on 32 A100s in the `ml-train-west` pool, which uses spot capacity. At 22:47 UTC last night the cloud provider reclaimed 12 of the nodes, which killed the distributed job, since every rank has to be present. The orchestrator's restart policy brought it back on a fresh set of nodes at 23:31, and it resumed from the checkpoint written at step 38,000, so we lost about 44 minutes of wall time and 1,400 steps of progress. I checked that the resume was real rather than a restart from scratch: the learning-rate schedule picked up at the right point in the cosine decay, the optimizer state loaded with matching shapes, and the training loss on the first logged step after resume was 0.412, against 0.409 just before the preemption, which is within normal noise. The data loader also resumed from the right shard, so no examples were seen twice.

V1 - **Confirmed the run resumed from the step 38,000 checkpoint with optimizer state and data position intact.** - The learning rate, loss, and shard index after resume match the values logged before the preemption.

S1 - **The ranking model retrain is at step 41,200 of 60,000.** - Throughput is 1.9 steps a second on the replacement nodes, which puts completion at about 04:00 UTC.

F1 - **Validation NDCG@10 at step 40,000 is 0.4731, against 0.4688 for the production model at the same step count.** - The gap has widened at every evaluation since step 20,000, which is the trend we wanted from the new click-debiasing features.

R1 - **Another preemption before 04:00 would cost up to 2,000 steps, about 18 minutes.** - Checkpoints are written every 2,000 steps, and the spot pool has seen two reclaims this week.

W1 - **When training finishes, the pipeline runs the offline evaluation suite and writes the comparison report.** - The suite covers NDCG, MRR, and the per-locale slices, and the report lands in `reports/ranking/2026-10-21/`; I'll read it and summarize the result against the shipping criteria.

C1 - **The NDCG lead so far is on the validation set only.** - The held-out test set and the per-locale slices run only after training finishes, and the German and Japanese slices regressed last time while the overall number improved.

Nothing needs a decision until the report exists. If the comparison clears the shipping criteria, the next step is the online A/B test, which needs your sign-off because it touches live search traffic, and I'll bring that to you with the numbers. If it doesn't, I'll look at which slices fell short before anything else.

The localized docs for the 5.0 release are partway through: Spanish and French are back from the translation vendor, reviewed, and merged, while German and Japanese are still with the vendor and due Friday.

The 5.0 release added 46 new pages and changed 112 existing ones, about 38,000 words of source text in total. I exported the changed strings through the translation management system on October 9, after the English freeze, and the vendor committed to delivering all four locales by October 24. Spanish and French came back on Monday. For each one I ran the localized build, the link checker, and the code-sample extractor, which confirms that code blocks weren't translated, since that's the most common vendor error. French had 17 code blocks where the vendor had translated comments inside shell commands, including one that turned `# required` into `# requis` in a YAML snippet users copy directly; harmless in that case, but I restored all 17 to the English source as the style guide requires. Spanish had six broken anchor links from translated heading slugs, which I fixed by adding explicit heading IDs. Both locales are now merged to `main` and live on the staging docs site.

AT1 - **Merged the Spanish and French translations for 5.0 after restoring 17 translated code blocks in French and fixing six broken anchors in Spanish.** - Both localized builds pass the link checker with zero errors, and the code-sample extractor reports every block identical to the English source.

S1 - **German and Japanese are with the translation vendor, due Friday, October 24.** - The vendor's portal shows German at 81% and Japanese at 64% translated, with review steps after both.

F1 - **Japanese is the likelier of the two to miss Friday.** - It's furthest behind, and the vendor's Japanese reviewer is shared with another client's release this week, per their project manager's note on Tuesday.

W1 - **When the vendor delivers German and Japanese, I'll run the same build, link, and code-block checks and merge them.** - The checks take about an hour per locale, and any fixes are usually the same two kinds I saw in French and Spanish.

B1 - **The Japanese glossary update waits on the Tokyo support team's review.** - Twelve new product terms need approved Japanese renderings; Aiko Sato on that team has the list and said she'll finish it Thursday, which the vendor needs before final review.

The release itself ships on October 28, and the docs site publishes whatever locales are merged by then; a locale that isn't ready falls back to English for the new pages, which the site handles with a banner. So the worst case for a late Japanese delivery is a few days of English pages in the Japanese docs, not a blocked release. Nothing here needs you right now: everything outstanding is with the vendor or the Tokyo team, and I'll report back when the last two locales are merged.
